newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid defence minister seeks forgiveness.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid defence minister seeks forgiveness.

text.p: Former defence minister Magnus Malan asked South Africa's truth commission for forgiveness on Wednesday but said digging up the past would do more harm than good.

General Malan, the most senior security chief from the apartheid era to testify to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, said he had never ordered or approved the assassination of political opponents.

But he acknowledged that in the mid-1980s he had set up the Civil Cooperation Bureau (CCB), a covert unit of the army's special forces whose official role was to disrupt Soviet-backed black liberation movements.

Malan, who volunteered to testify but refuses to apply for indemnity from prosecution for any of his actions, said he regretted the death of civilians caught in the crossfire during army raids into neighbouring countries.

"I wish to state clearly that I take moral responsibility for the actions of members of the South African defence force during the periods when I was involved ... where members acted unlawfully, I wish to offer my unqualified apologies," he said.
Malan, 67, who was armed forces chief from 1976 to 1980 and then defence minister until 1991, said the actions of his troops had to be seen in the context of Soviet attempts at global domination.
"I and most of my generals are in the autumn of our lives. It is understanding and forgiveness we really seek, not legal pardons," he said.

Malan, who was acquitted last year on charges that he was behind the 1987 political killing of 13 blacks suspected of supporting the ruling African National Congress, told the commission there was little point in raking over old history.
"By your incessant probing into the past you may create a reaction which will be difficult to control ... Let not our past destroy our future," he said.
Archbishop Desmond Tutu, chairman of the commission, told Malan that South Africa could not build a future on a foundation of untruth.
"The objective of the commission is not to push someone into a corner. We want the truth for the sake of healing," Tutu said.

Malan and members of the commission engaged in heated exchanges over several issues, including allegations that a shadowy third force had carried out political murders and that the CCB was responsible among things for murdering lawyer Anton Lubowski in Namibia in the 1980s.
"No third force ever existed," Malan said, refusing to answer some questions from the commission unless they were put in writing, and he was given time to research the answers.
He said the death of civilians in crossfire was part of the ugly reality of war.
"However I never issued an order for the assassination of anybody ... the killing of political opponents of the government never formed part of the brief of the defence force," he said.
Malan is believed to have been persuaded to testify to the commission by his former president P.W. Botha, one of only two surviving white heads of state from the apartheid era.
Political analysts have said Botha and Malan might have been concerned that without such testimony, the commission's final report might lean too heavily against the country's former white rulers.
The analysts said the report was certain to be widely cited in campaigning for the next general election, due in 1999.
